svg.title: Distinct rows and seat positions give different counts for sharing a row and sitting adjacent
svg.desc: Eight distinct people A through H occupy two physical rows, Front and Back, each with four distinct seats. In one displayed arrangement the front row is A C B D and the back row is E F G H. A and B share a row but are not adjacent. In the second arrangement the front row is C A B D with the same back row, so A and B are adjacent. Every seat is individually labelled F one to F four or B one to B four. To count all seatings with A and B in the same row, choose one of two rows, choose two of the other six people to join them, then arrange each row in four factorial ways. The count is two times six choose two times four factorial squared, seventeen thousand two hundred eighty. To count adjacent A and B, choose one of two rows, one of three neighbouring seat-pairs within that row, one of two orders for A and B, and arrange the remaining six people in six factorial ways. This gives eight thousand six hundred forty. Adjacency is a subset of sharing a row, so the conditional probability of adjacency given a shared row is one half under uniform seatings. There is no adjacency across rows. The Front and Back rows retain their identities even though both contain four seats; no division for exchanging the two rows is made.
